entries.title: The exosome prion chain
entries.claim: Prion-bearing extracellular vesicles transmit disease to animals.
entries.subject: Prions
entries.stage_note: trace complete; 8/8 verified at source. The hypothesis is open, not the trace: the claim as worded depends on vesicle enclosure, which Entry 011 records as untested.
entries.summary: 8-node trace, all verified at source. The pellet transmits; whether the infectivity is inside the vesicles is an open question (Entry 011).
entries.plain_status: Material from the preparation called exosomes causes disease when injected into the brains of PrP-overexpressing mice, in two independent studies. Whether that material is carried inside vesicles, rather than as free aggregate pelleting alongside them, has not been established.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC

entries.title: The origin of Santa Claus
entries.claim: Santa Claus is a real figure who delivers gifts to children everywhere on one night.
entries.subject: Santa Claus
entries.stage_note: trail mapped; sources not yet verified
entries.summary: Origin trail: St. Nicholas of Myra → Sinterklaas → Moore (1823) → Nast → Coca-Cola. A worked example of tracing a claim to its source — mid-trace.
entries.plain_status: Taken literally — one figure, all children, one night — not supported. The figure's origin is real and datable; that trace is in progress.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC

entries.title: Chronic wasting disease and humans
entries.claim: Chronic wasting disease (CWD) can transmit to humans and cause prion disease.
entries.subject: Chronic wasting disease
entries.stage_note: trace complete; all sources verified at source
entries.summary: CWD-to-human transmission. No confirmed human case. Transmission studies conflict across models, isolates and routes.
entries.plain_status: No confirmed human case has been reported. Transmission studies report conflicting results across different models, isolates and routes.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC (AI-assisted research; sources re-checked at publisher 9–12 Oct 2026)

entries.title: The UK appendix prion surveys
entries.claim: Abnormal prion protein found in UK appendix tissue (about 1 in 2,000 people) indicates incubating variant CJD infection.
entries.subject: Variant CJD
entries.stage_note: all five sources read in full at source; stage held at Under Investigation while three citation DOIs, corrected 12 Oct 2026, are re-checked against the nodes they support
entries.summary: UK surveys found abnormal prion protein in ~1 in 2,000 appendixes. Whether that is incubating vCJD is unresolved; the settling experiment is funded but unreported.
entries.plain_status: Abnormal prion protein is present in appendix tissue at about 1 in 2,000. Whether it means incubating vCJD is unresolved: one molecular test leans against it, the direct infectivity test found no transmission from the fixed survey positives, and the amplification test on the positive specimens has not been reported.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC (AI-assisted research; sources re-checked at publisher 9–12 Oct 2026)

entries.title: The autoclave parameters for human prions
entries.claim: The recommended steam-sterilisation parameters (134°C for 18 minutes) inactivate human prions on surgical instruments.
entries.subject: Prion decontamination
entries.stage_note: 3 of 4 sources verified at source; the 1994 decontamination study usually cited for the figure is paywalled (located, not read)
entries.summary: The most-quoted autoclave figure (134°C/18 min) is not tied to a cited inactivation experiment; a single steam cycle leaves residual sporadic-CJD infectivity, while chemical and two-step methods work.
entries.plain_status: The 134°C / 18-minute figure is in the WHO guidance, which cites no inactivation study for it and concedes incomplete removal in worst cases. A readable 2026 bioassay shows a single 134°C cycle does not eliminate one sporadic-CJD strain; chemical and combination treatments do better.
not_linked: 004 — both concern prion safety policy and both sit in Public Health, but neither's evidence depends on the other. The shared field is the accurate connection; a rests_on link would overstate it.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC (AI-assisted research; sources checked at publisher 9 Oct 2026)

entries.title: The appendix-assay false-positive rate
entries.claim: The amplification assay proposed to test the UK appendix-survey positives has a measured false-positive rate on known-negative appendix tissue.
entries.subject: Variant CJD
entries.stage_note: key method paper verified at source; the claim is a documented gap, not a positive finding
entries.summary: The assay proposed to test the UK appendix-survey positives has no measured false-positive rate on negative appendix; its validation used a handful of non-CJD controls, not a quantified specificity.
entries.plain_status: The amplification method proposed to test the ~1-in-2,000 appendix positives was validated against a small non-CJD control set that did not amplify. Its specificity — a false-positive rate on known-negative survey-era appendix — has not been quantified, and the assay's substrate is built for one genotype most survey positives do not share.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC (AI-assisted research; sources checked at publisher 9 Oct 2026)

entries.title: Codon 129 and kuru selection
entries.claim: Balancing selection, driven by prehistoric kuru-like epidemics, shaped codon 129 of the human prion protein gene worldwide.
entries.subject: PRNP codon 129
entries.stage_note: all three chain sources verified at source, the last two read from the original papers on 12 Oct 2026
entries.summary: Codon 129 selection. Demonstrated in the Fore within living memory. The species-wide claim rests on a disputed statistical signal; no through-time test has been run.
entries.plain_status: Kuru is documented to have selected codon 129 in one population (the Fore) within living memory. Whether similar selection acted across human prehistory worldwide is unproven; the original statistical evidence did not survive resequencing.
not_linked: 001 — shares Molecular Neuroscience, but this entry's argument does not rest on exosome transmission. The overlap is the phrase 'unrelated to prions' in What would settle it, not a dependency.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC (AI-assisted research; sources checked at publisher 9 Oct 2026)

entries.title: The PRNP balancing-selection signal
entries.claim: The worldwide signal of balancing selection at the prion protein gene is real, not an artefact of how the variants were sampled.
entries.subject: PRNP selection signal
entries.stage_note: Mead 2003 read at source 12 Oct 2026, including Table 2; three of six chain sources still read at abstract only
entries.summary: Is the PRNP balancing-selection signal real? The high-frequency-variant signal did not survive rare-variant resequencing; attributed to ascertainment bias. Authors partly conceded. PRNP absent from current canonical lists.
entries.plain_status: The original positive Tajima's D signal did not survive resequencing that captured rare variants. Reanalyses attribute it to ascertainment bias; the original authors partly conceded the statistics. A different signal (positive or purifying selection) may still be present.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC (AI-assisted research; sources checked at publisher 9 Oct 2026)

entries.title: Atypical BSE and spontaneous origin
entries.claim: Atypical BSE (H-type and L-type) arises spontaneously in cattle, rather than from an infectious or feed-borne source.
entries.subject: Atypical BSE
entries.stage_note: all nine chain sources verified at source; Biacabe 2004, the last one, read from the original paper on 12 Oct 2026
entries.summary: Atypical BSE spontaneous origin. Written into the international BSE framework as a belief. Supporting evidence is circumstantial; the defining test has not been run.
entries.plain_status: International animal-health rules treat atypical BSE as spontaneous. The rules themselves say \"believed\"; a 2016 review calls the assumption \"still mainly speculative\"; no test has settled it.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC (AI-assisted research; sources checked at publisher 9 Oct 2026)

entries.title: Cross-seeding as true templating
entries.claim: One misfolded protein cross-seeds a different protein by acting as a structural template (true heterotypic templating), rather than by an indirect route.
entries.subject: Protein cross-seeding
entries.stage_note: 7 of 8 chain sources verified at source; one (Rasmussen 2018, the key negative) read at abstract and title only — full text behind a publisher browser check
entries.summary: Protein cross-seeding. Readily shown in vitro at high concentrations. Whether it is true templating or an indirect effect is unresolved; the clearest animal studies point to an indirect route.
entries.plain_status: Cross-seeding between two amyloid proteins is easy to show in a test tube and harder in animals. Whether it works by one protein templating another, or by an indirect route, is unresolved, and the two best-controlled mouse studies of the main pair concluded against direct templating.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC (AI-assisted research; sources checked at publisher 9 Oct 2026)

entries.title: Prion infectivity inside extracellular vesicles
entries.claim: The prion infectivity recovered in extracellular-vesicle preparations is enclosed inside the vesicles, rather than free aggregate co-pelleting with them.
entries.subject: Prion vesicle enclosure
entries.stage_note: Soukup 2023 read in full at source 12 Oct 2026; both quoted sentences confirmed. The claim stays open because no experiment has separated enclosed from co-pelleting material and assayed each for infectivity
entries.summary: Prion preparations called \"exosomes\" are a pellet that also contains free prion aggregate. Whether the infectivity is inside vesicles is untested, and the standard localisation assay cannot settle it.
entries.plain_status: Prion material is recovered from the fraction labelled \"exosomes\", and that fraction transmits disease. Whether the infectious material is inside the vesicles, or free clumps of prion protein that settle at the same speed, has not been established — and the test the field normally uses cannot answer it.
not_linked: 010 — shares Biochemistry, and both ask whether material is what its label says. But cross-seeding is about templating between proteins and this is about where a protein sits; neither's evidence bears on the other. The shared field is the accurate connection.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC (AI-assisted research; drafted from the project's Prion Research Notes, sources not yet pulled)

entries.title: Open-access flags and the papers behind them
entries.claim: A paper flagged open access by the major bibliographic indexes can be read in full at the location they give.
entries.subject: Open-access metadata
entries.stage_note: both nodes verified at source — they are the registry's own direct observations, so there is no citation chain outstanding. The hypothesis stays open: the rate is unmeasured, and a first sample of 600 records found no second case
entries.summary: An index saying a paper is free is a claim about a file, not about a readable paper. One verified case where the file is an image; the rate is unmeasured, and our first sample of 600 found no second case.
entries.plain_status: Three large indexes told us a paper was free to read. The file all three pointed at was a photograph of one figure, not the paper. How often that happens is not known — our own first count of 600 records found no other case like it.
not_linked: 010 — Rasmussen 2018 is the paper this entry's counterexample concerns, but 010's argument is about protein cross-seeding and does not depend on anything here. The connection is that this entry explains why 010's node is marked Unreadable.
entries.author: Priority Nexus LLC (AI-assisted research; the counterexample and the sample were produced directly from the named APIs on 12 October 2026)
entries.conflicts: This entry arose from the registry's own work. The counterexample was found while trying to read a source for Entry 010, and the measurement below was run by the registry rather than taken from a published study.
